newsitem.title: USA: "British bandits" rob ritzy Washington-area homes.
newsitem.headline: "British bandits" rob ritzy Washington-area homes.

text.p: A pair of so-called "British bandits" armed with handguns have robbed at least eight homes in some of Washington's lushest suburban neighbourhoods, police said on Monday.

From Sir Galahad Way to Stapleford Hall Drive to the latest robbery near the Manor Country Club, the two have been consistent: they wear black, cover their faces and speak with British or Australian accents, said Col. George Ludington of the Montgomery County police department, which serves the Maryland suburbs where the robberies took place.
"The problem here is, they go in looking for a confrontation," Ludington said by telephone. "They wake you up in the middle of the night with a gun in your face."
The two men, described by police as white, in their mid-30s and about 6 feet (1.8 metres) tall, always strike between 3:30 a.m. and 6 a.m.

"They demand cash. They don't want other valuables, all they want is cash. In a couple of cases they didn't get any ... When they get the cash, they always leave by the way they came," Ludington said.
Ludington was unamused by the "British" nickname given the bandits in local news accounts. "We just call them criminals," he said.

The armed robberies began on Jan. 25 and the latest one was Sunday morning. The first seven were at veritable estates outside Washington: large homes with large grounds, often with security systems and guard dogs.
The robbers often entered through open garages or unlocked doors, Ludington said.
The eighth robbery was in a more typical suburban neighbourhood, he said.

The Washington Post characterised the robbers as unusually polite, describing one case where they left a home empty-handed when the residents could only find a total of $6 in cash. Ludington could not confirm this incident.
No injuries were reported, but Ludington feared that could change.

"The groundwork's being set here for a real tragedy," he said. "We don't know what makes them tick ... the law of averages says that one of the homes they enter, the owner's going to be a gun owner and there could be a gun battle right there."
Ludington said the robbers may have hit other homes where victims did not report the crimes.
